events.title: C++17 standardized
events.summary: ISO published [C++]17 in December 2017 — adding `std::optional`, `std::variant`, structured bindings, and parallel algorithms.
events.about: [C++]17 brought everyday ergonomics game engines and finance code needed: optional values without pointer sentinels, `if (auto x = map.find(key))` bindings, and filesystem library in the standard. It bridged the gap between [C++]11's foundation and [C++]20's larger features.

narrative.whyChosen: [C++]17 delivered practical quality-of-life features used across industry codebases.
narrative.whyImportant: Optional, variant, and structured bindings reduced boilerplate and bug classes.
narrative.problemSolved: [C++]11 was powerful but verbose; teams needed smaller, composable standard-library tools.

events.title: MakerDAO launches DAI stablecoin
events.summary: MakerDAO launched the DAI stablecoin on December 18, 2017 — a dollar-pegged asset backed by overcollateralized ether locked in [smart contract]s.
events.about: Users deposited ETH into Maker vaults and minted DAI against it — no bank account required. DAI became DeFi's unit of account for lending, trading, and payroll before centralized stablecoins dominated volume. It showed algorithmic collateral could hold a peg — until black swans tested the design.

narrative.whyChosen: DAI was the first widely used decentralized stablecoin on Ethereum.
narrative.whyImportant: It gave DeFi protocols a trust-minimized dollar substitute.
narrative.problemSolved: Traders needed stable value on-chain without off-ramping to banks for every trade.

events.title: FCC votes to repeal net neutrality rules
events.summary: The FCC voted 3–2 on December 14, 2017 to repeal the 2015 Open Internet Order — ending Title II classification of broadband and returning ISPs to lighter-touch regulation.
events.about: Chairman Ajit Pai's Restoring Internet Freedom Order let ISPs theoretically block, throttle, or prioritize traffic again — though major providers largely pledged not to. States like California passed their own net neutrality laws; startups worried about paid peering deals affecting latency-sensitive apps. The repeal remained politically contested through subsequent FCC administrations.

narrative.whyChosen: The 2017 repeal reversed the strongest federal net neutrality protections U.S. developers had.
narrative.whyImportant: It shifted broadband regulation to state-by-state patchwork and renewed [ISP] lobbying battles.
narrative.problemSolved: ISPs argued Title II rules discouraged infrastructure investment; advocates feared fast-lane discrimination.
